mechanism.rule: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Commercial Refrigerators, Freezers, and Refrigerator-Freezers (DOE final rule, RIN 1904-AD82, Docket EERE-2017-BT-STD-0007, 10 CFR part 431)
mechanism.agency: Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, Department of Energy
mechanism.required: <cite index="31-2">DOE adopted new and amended energy conservation standards for commercial refrigeration equipment (CRE).</cite> <cite index="13-1">Manufacturers had to comply with the new and amended standards on and after January 22, 2029.</cite> The standards bind manufacturers of CRE. DOE adopted trial standard level (TSL) 3. <cite index="10-3,10-9">On March 7, 2025, DOE delayed the effective date from March 24, 2025 to May 20, 2025 (90 FR 11466). The compliance date stayed January 22, 2029.</cite> The resolution did not amend the standards. It disapproved the rule, so that <cite index="8-3,8-5">the rule (90 FR 7464, published January 21, 2025) has no force or effect.</cite>
mechanism.benefits: DOE's own figures from the final rule (30-year analysis period, equipment shipped 2029–2058, 2023 dollars). (1) Consumer benefit: <cite index="59-2">the cumulative net present value of total consumer benefits is $1.32 billion at a 7% discount rate and $3.43 billion at 3%.</cite> (2) Health benefit: <cite index="59-6">the monetized value of reduced SO2 and NOx emissions at TSL 3 is $0.86 billion at 7% and $2.19 billion at 3%.</cite> (3) Energy savings: <cite index="63-1,63-2,63-3">full-fuel-cycle energy savings over 2029–2058 are 1.11 quads, about 6.5% of the energy use of this equipment.</cite> (4) Emissions: <cite index="68-6">cumulative reductions of 19.7 million metric tons of CO2, 6.0 thousand tons of SO2 and 36.9 thousand tons of NOx.</cite> (5) Purchasers: <cite index="63-9">about 91% of affected CRE purchasers would see a net benefit or not be affected at TSL 3.</cite> (6) Net benefits: <cite index="58-7">including the manufacturer loss, and calculated using the 2023 SC-GHG estimates, annualized net benefits would be $537–540 million at a 3% discount rate and $444–447 million at 7%.</cite> DOE also reports a separate, lower net benefit using the 2021 interim SC-GHG estimates.
mechanism.costs: DOE's own figures from the same analysis. (1) Manufacturers: <cite index="63-5">DOE estimated industry net present value (INPV) without new standards at $3,022.3 million (2023$).</cite> <cite index="59-7">At TSL 3 the projected INPV change was a decrease of about $77.8 million to $51.3 million, or 2.6% to 1.7%.</cite> (2) Purchasers: the NPV figures above are the estimated value of future operating-cost savings minus the estimated increased equipment costs. About 91% of purchasers would see a net benefit or be unaffected, so roughly 9% would have had a net cost. A garbled excerpt of the rule suggests payback periods of <cite index="30-10">0.9 to 7.0 years across equipment classes.</cite> (3) The rule excerpts reviewed do not include DOE's annualized incremental equipment cost line, so it is not stated here.
mechanism.agency_reasons: <cite index="13-3">DOE determined that the new and amended standards would result in significant energy conservation and are technologically feasible and economically justified.</cite> <cite index="68-5">EPCA requires DOE to periodically review existing standards to see whether more-stringent standards would be technologically feasible, economically justified and save significant energy.</cite>
mechanism.sponsor_reasons: Rep. Craig Goldman (R-TX), the sponsor: his office said <cite index="43-4">DOE estimated the standards would impose an $8 billion burden on small businesses and consumers.</cite> The $8 billion figure could not be verified in the DOE rule text retrieved. House Energy and Commerce Chairmen Guthrie and Latta said the rule was <cite index="46-4">needless regulation raising prices for businesses and families while failing to provide cost savings or increasing food safety.</cite> The Energy and Commerce release also said <cite index="46-11">DOE itself estimated that at least one standard would have a payback period of more than 90 years.</cite> That figure also could not be verified in the rule text retrieved.
mechanism.status: Became law. <cite index="53-7,53-8">President Trump signed the resolution on May 9, 2025, so the rule has no force or effect.</cite> <cite index="53-9">On May 20, 2025 DOE withdrew the rule and gave notice that its standards have no force or effect (90 FR 21392).</cite> The rule is void.

outcomes.claim: After the resolution became law, DOE withdrew the January 2025 final rule from the Federal Register. The amended CRE standards in that rule never took legal effect. DOE's withdrawal notice records that the joint resolution of disapproval was signed May 9, 2025, and that, under the Congressional Review Act, the rule shall have no force or effect.
outcomes.quote: As a result, DOE withdraws the January 2025 Final Rule and provides notice that the amended energy conservation standards for commercial refrigerators, freezers, and refrigerator-freezers prescribed in the January 2025 Final Rule shall have no force or effect.
outcomes.counterpoint: This records the legal status only. It is not a measured effect on prices, energy use or businesses.

outcomes.claim: Benefits forgone, per DOE's pre-vote estimate. Over 2029–2058 shipments the standards were projected to deliver consumer net present value of $1.32 billion (7% discount rate) to $3.43 billion (3%), plus health benefits of $0.86–2.19 billion. They were also projected to save 1.11 quads of full-fuel-cycle energy and cut CO2 by 19.7 million metric tons. About 91% of affected purchasers would see a net benefit or not be affected. This is a forecast, not a measured outcome. Whether these savings are in fact forgone depends on what purchasers and manufacturers do without the rule.

source.title: Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Commercial Refrigerators, Freezers, and Refrigerator-Freezers (final rule)

outcomes.counterpoint: DOE's published consumer NPV is positive at both discount rates.

outcomes.claim: Burden lifted, per DOE's pre-vote estimate. Manufacturers avoided a projected INPV loss of about $51.3–77.8 million (1.7–2.6% of a $3,022.3 million baseline, 2023$). About 9% of affected purchasers would have faced a net cost, since DOE estimated 91% would see a net benefit or not be affected. The compliance cost would have started in 2029.
outcomes.quote: DOE estimates the change in INPV to range from -2.6 percent to -1.7 percent, which is approximately -$77.8 million to -$51.3 million.
outcomes.counterpoint: DOE judged the manufacturer loss small against the benefits.

notes: (1) The figures come from search-result excerpts of the Federal Register and DOE documents. I did not open the full text or the Regulatory Impact Analysis / Technical Support Document, and some excerpts were garbled. Check the figures before publication, especially the 0.9–7.0 year payback range, the full-fuel-cycle energy savings at TSL 3, and DOE's annualized incremental equipment cost, which I did not retrieve. (2) DOE's INPV low-end figure appears as $78.7 million in one copy and about $77.8 million in another. (3) Third-party figures differ from DOE's consumer NPV of $1.32–3.43 billion. An advocacy group (Appliance Standards Awareness Project) cited nearly $4.6 billion in utility-bill savings over 30 years, as reported by the Washington Examiner. Nine state AGs cited $4.61 billion. I could not reconcile these with DOE's own numbers, so I did not use them as outcomes. (4) The $8 billion and 90-year payback claims are sponsor statements I could not trace to the DOE rule. (5) The effective date is given as the originally stated March 24, 2025. It was delayed to May 20, 2025, the day DOE withdrew the rule, and the rule never took effect. (6) The search results do not record what followed the withdrawal. I found no agency data, GAO or inspector general report, or peer-reviewed study on prices, energy use or business effects. The compliance date was 2029, so little could be measured yet. The search results do not show whether later DOE action restored or replaced the standards. This is a valid finding, not a gap to fill with inference. (7) The Congress.gov excerpt shows the Senate passage vote as 52-45. I did not retrieve the Senate roll-call pages for the motion to proceed (52-46) or the House roll call, so those counts are taken from the brief.
